verdicts.reasons: Version A strictly adheres to the 5-minute time constraint and judge's moderate speed preference (estimated at 290 seconds), whereas Version B is over time (312 seconds) and spreads itself too thin by trying to revive extraneous arguments like 50-state fiat theory and a second permutation. Version A follows the team strategy notes faithfully, efficiently grouping the 2NC's permutation arguments on the counterplan, pressing the interstate compact shift and solvency deficits, and cleanly dismantling the Climate Tradeoff DA.

B keeps more offense alive: it extends the dropped 50-state fiat theory, 'the CP links too,' and the conceded Parkinson answer. It also answers the simultaneity and sequencing claims directly by defending the backstop perm (a backstop acts only after states fail). A ignores the second perm and those drops. B adds a strong 'even if' against the new compact (fifty-state negotiation is slow) and turns ELI into proof the perm works. The main costs are that B runs about 12 seconds over for a judge who wants moderate speed, so it needs a trim, while A fits the time comfortably but gives up strategic leverage.

Version A makes sharper offensive moves against the block's evidence. It argues that a compact with the force of federal law needs Congressional consent, so the CP links to its own net benefit. It turns Adler on cross-border streams and uses Parkinson's line that developed economies need little incremental water investment. It also flips Sundaram & Popov onto the 1AC's economic-decline impact to answer no water wars. Version B covers similar ground more thinly: it mislabels the States CP as a process CP to invoke the judge's lean, claims theory was dropped when the 2NC's goldilocks argument answered it, and its case section barely answers the 1NR's no-water-wars extension.

Version B generates more offensive clash from the neg's own evidence. It argues the compact needs congressional consent, so the CP links to its own net benefit. It flips Adler into support for federal action on cross-border streams, and it uses Parkinson's 'little investment for developed economies' line to undercut the link. Version A covers the flow comparably and uses the judge's process-CP lean nicely. However, its perm and DA answers are more defensive, and its 'block never answered theory' claim is thinner. B also sensibly narrows to perm do both and cross-applies Sundaram & Popov to the economic-decline advantage, and it still fits within time.

Version A keeps more strategic options alive: it extends the dropped 50-state fiat theory and the 'CP links too' argument, which eliminates the net benefit independently of winning no link. It also extends the backstop perm against the sequencing claim. Version B fits the time limit and gives deeper warrants on Troutman, Parkinson and the ELI floor, but it forfeits theory and the CP-links argument. A runs roughly 12 seconds over, so it needs trimming, but that is a small fix compared with the offense B concedes.

Version A exceeds the 300-second time limit (estimated at 312 s), which directly violates the explicit paradigm instruction to write less rather than speed up, risking the judge cutting off the case debate entirely. Version B fits cleanly within the time limit at 290 s while delivering substantially better warranted clash, particularly in using the internal text of ELI and Parkinson to dismantle the CP solvency and DA links. While Version A points out the dropped 50-state fiat theory, Version B's strategic choices, depth of evidence comparison, and time discipline make it far more effective in securing the ballot.

Version B is tactically superior and makes better use of the five-minute time limit by avoiding reading a lengthy card that eats up precious 1AR time. Instead of reading Roper, B generates devastating analytical presses on the interstate compact—notably pointing out that compacts require congressional consent, which turns the Neg's own 'federal action' link argument against the counterplan. Furthermore, B exploits specific conceded evidence exceptionally well, citing the text of the Neg's Parkinson card (developed economies need little incremental investment) to eliminate the DA, capitalizing on the 2NC drop on 50-state fiat theory, and cleanly turning the new 1NR economic downturn impact.

Version B is a masterclass in 1AR execution. Strategically cross-applying the negative's newly read Sundaram and Popov downturn card to Advantage 1's economic decline impact brilliantly solves the water wars defense, and quoting Parkinson's warrant that developed economies need minimal incremental water investment completely dismantles the DA's internal link. Version B also handles the CP more cleanly by distinguishing which 2NC answers applied exclusively to the backstop permutation and demonstrating how an interstate compact triggers congressional approval and the DA.

B's compact answer is the strongest single argument on the flow. It notes a compact needs congressional consent, so the CP includes federal action and links to its own net benefit. B also turns Parkinson using the card's own 'little incremental investment for developed economies' line and adds a durability warrant (statutory caps, the Wisconsin rollback). A's perm defense leans on 'the CP links too,' which is weak against a federal budget tradeoff. A does read the Roper compacts-fail card, a real plus, but its theory extension undercuts itself with 'reject the argument' and its warrants are thinner overall.

Version A executes elite technical policy debate strategy. It weaponizes the 1NR's new Sundaram & Popov card to supply an uncontested terminal impact to Advantage 1's economic decline claim, cites the exact text of Parkinson to decisively dismantle the DA's internal link, and points out that an interstate compact requires congressional approval (linking the CP directly to its own net benefit). Version B is solid, but Version A's evidence comparisons and strategic turns create a clean, lethal path to the ballot in the 2AR.

B's perm answer is more robust: it argues the counterplan links to the enforcement-cost DA too, so there is no net benefit. A's version depends entirely on winning DA defense. B also answers the new 2NC compact with the team's own Roper 'compacts fail' card while flagging it as new. A has a clever congressional-consent point and stronger race-to-the-bottom detail (the Wisconsin rollback, Parkinson on developed economies), but B's net-benefit framing better protects the perm, despite a small concession on theory.

Version A is vastly more strategic and time-efficient. It capitalizes on the 2NC's complete drop of 50-state fiat theory as a voting issue, whereas Version B unnecessarily dilutes the argument by suggesting the judge just 'reject the argument.' Additionally, Version A's technical collapse on the CP and DA is superior: it cross-applies the Neg's own ELI evidence to dismantle the Troutman link to the perm and exploits the text of Parkinson on the DA, while Version B wastes nearly a minute reading a Roper card in a time-crunched 1AR and advances a nonsensical 'CP links too' argument against a federal budget tradeoff.

Version B reads the 'CP links too' argument, which takes away the net benefit on the only DA backing the counterplan. It also preempts the interstate-compact solvency shift with Roper '15, the compact evidence the 2NC's compact claims rely on. And it turns the neg's own ELI card ('no more stringent than') into a deficit. Version A has deeper DA and case analytics, plus a sequenced perm that anticipates the 2NC timing argument, but omitting the CP-links-too and compact answers leaves bigger strategic gaps; both fit the time and are flowable at moderate speed.

Both versions answer every 1NC argument. B does more with the same time: the perms are explained through the neg's own Berry & Huckins and ELI evidence, the DA answers are more developed (it demands a plan-specific link, notes there is no line item, and indicts the text of Parkinson), and the CP-links argument is tied to Parkinson's finite-investment logic. A spends time on a preemptive compacts-fail card before the 1NC text mentions a compact, and on Chernoff, whose generic prediction theory is only loosely responsive. B instead answers no water wars directly: the cooperation evidence is about international rivers and does not reach the domestic economic and drinking-water impacts.

Version A is vastly superior in technical execution, coverage, and strategic awareness. It aligns closely with the actual round flow and strategy notes by maintaining offensive pressure on the DA ('CP links too'), executing the planned solvency extensions, reading Chernoff 9 on case, and presciently pre-empting the interstate compact defense with Roper 15. In contrast, Version B drops Chernoff, drops the CP link turn, and carelessly includes unedited meta-instruction notes at the bottom of the speech.

Version B gives deeper, more flowable warrants. Its sequenced backstop perm pre-empts the 2NC's simultaneity and sequencing answers, and its no-link explicitly addresses enforcement costs. It also adds probability impact calculus and reciprocity on 50-state fiat, and its case answers are three-part and specific. Version A has useful breadth (the 'CP links too' argument and a Roper compact pre-empt), but its perms and case answers are thinner, and its Chernoff water-wars answer barely engages the argument.

Version B is strategically superior because it explicitly extends 1AC solvency, executes the 'CP links too' argument on the Tradeoff DA to eliminate the net benefit, and reads Chernoff 9 to fortify the case impact against the 1NC's water wars defense. Version A entirely omits an extension of 1AC solvency, leaves out the CP link turn on the DA, and fails to introduce Roper to contest the neg's compact mechanism.

Version A's analytics are more warranted and comparative. It explains why the perm leaves the net benefit near zero, reads Parkinson against the neg with specifics, and runs a detailed argument that the CP links to the DA using Parkinson's finite-investment logic. It also answers water wars by separating our domestic impacts from their international cooperation evidence. Version B's preemptive Roper compacts card proved useful once the 2NC went for a compact, but its DA answers are thinner (non-unique and no impact are one or two lines) and it spends time on the generic Chernoff card, so A gives this flow-focused judge clearer, better-warranted answers.

Version B is far better aligned with the round's trajectory and strategic needs: it introduces the critical Chernoff and Fitzsimmons evidence to defend the case impact against the 1NC water wars defense (which the 1NR directly engages), and it reads the 'CP with federal backstop' perm that correctly matches the flow. Version B also smartly anticipates the 2NC's shift to interstate compacts by reading the Roper card on the CP flow, creating massive solvency pressure while comfortably fitting under the 8-minute time limit.

Version B demonstrates superior strategic allocation and warrant depth. Version A wastes nearly two minutes reading two superfluous cards—a 57-second indict of interstate compacts that the 1NC never explicitly fiated, and a redundant 42-second epistemology card on case—squeezing analytics on the DA. Version B smartly holds the compact card for the 1AR, provides much richer analytical clash on the DA and Perms, and explicitly extends 1AC solvency on case.

Version B warrants its arguments more thoroughly. It turns the neg's own ELI and Parkinson cards against them, with Parkinson's developed-economies line gutting the DA link and ELI's alterable statutes supporting a durability deficit. Its case answers are analytic and on point: alt causes don't deny solvency, wetlands filter runoff, and the uncontested economic-decline impact survives no water wars. Version A leans on Chernoff and Fitzsimmons, prediction-theory cards that fit poorly against a no-water-wars argument; its preemptive Roper 'compacts fail' card is a smart hedge against the 2NC compact but doesn't outweigh B's stronger clash and clearer explanation for a moderate-speed judge.

Version B demonstrates superior strategic efficiency and round awareness, choosing deep, responsive analytics on case and the DA rather than burning nearly two minutes on generic prediction cards (Chernoff/Fitzsimmons) and preempting an interstate compact argument that wasn't in the 1NC. Version B also smartly leverages the judge's specific paradigm against judge kick, utilizes devastating close-read indicts of the 1NC's Parkinson and ELI evidence, and properly executes the team strategy within the judge's moderate speed constraints.

Version A answers the case with warranted analytics: it turns the frequency claim and flags the uncontested economic impact. Version B spends case time reading Chernoff and Fitzsimmons, prediction-methodology cards that don't actually engage 'no water wars.' A also does more comparative work with the neg's own evidence (ELI's statutory 'no more stringent than' concession as a durability deficit, Parkinson's developed-economies line) and uses the judge's no-judge-kick preference strategically. B's Roper compacts-fail preempt is a smart addition, but its perm explanations are muddier, e.g. the 'DA link identical under the CP' line.

Version A demonstrates significantly better time and resource management. Version B burns 57 seconds reading Roper '15 to answer an interstate compact argument that the 1NC never introduced, putting severe time pressure on the rest of the speech and forcing superficial analytics on the Climate Tradeoff DA. Version A strategically holds premature cards, provides substantially deeper clash on the Parkinson card and the regulatory mechanism of the plan, and fits comfortably within the time constraints of a judge who prefers moderate pace and clear analytics.
